clinicalPearls: SCA11 is a rare autosomal dominant, largely pure cerebellar ataxia caused by truncating (frameshift or nonsense) mutations in TTBK2, the gene encoding tau tubulin kinase 2.
It is among the mildest of the dominant ataxias, with slowly progressive gait and limb ataxia, prolonged preservation of walking and a normal or near-normal lifespan.
Onset is usually in adolescence or early adulthood, although some individuals present in mid-life.
Eye-movement abnormalities are characteristic and helpful clues: horizontal and vertical nystagmus, jerky smooth pursuit and abnormal saccades.
Mild dysarthria and pyramidal signs (brisk reflexes, occasional extensor plantar responses) may accompany the cerebellar syndrome, but marked extracerebellar disease argues against SCA11.
MRI typically shows isolated vermian and hemispheric cerebellar atrophy with a relatively preserved brainstem.
TTBK2 governs assembly of the primary cilium, placing SCA11 among cilium-related neurodegenerations and distinguishing its mechanism from the repeat-expansion ataxias.
Diagnosis relies on the dominant family history and targeted TTBK2 sequencing after the common repeat-expansion ataxias have been excluded.
reference.pathophysiology: SCA11 is caused by heterozygous truncating mutations in TTBK2 on chromosome 15q, which encodes tau tubulin kinase 2, a serine-threonine kinase. TTBK2 is recruited to the distal end of the mother centriole (the basal body), where it initiates primary cilium assembly by displacing the capping protein CP110 and recruiting intraflagellar transport machinery, and it also phosphorylates tau and tubulin. Disease-causing mutations truncate the protein, preserving the amino-terminal kinase domain but removing the carboxy-terminal regulatory region; the truncated product is thought to act through a dominant-negative effect and/or haploinsufficiency, impairing ciliogenesis and disturbing Purkinje cell homeostasis. The result is a comparatively slow, selective cerebellar degeneration with Purkinje cell loss, which underlies the mild and predominantly cerebellar clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: SCA6 (CACNA1A) — slowly progressive, relatively pure late-onset cerebellar ataxia
SCA5 (SPTBN2) and SCA26 (EEF2) — dominant pure cerebellar ataxias
SCA15/16 (ITPR1) — very slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia
Sporadic adult-onset cerebellar ataxia and the cerebellar variant of multiple system atrophy
Acquired ataxias (alcohol-related, gluten, paraneoplastic) as treatable mimics
additionalInvestigations: Targeted TTBK2 gene sequencing, usually within an ataxia gene panel or exome analysis
Repeat-sizing to exclude the common expansion ataxias (SCA1, 2, 3, 6, 7 and others)
Brain MRI to document cerebellar atrophy and exclude structural or brainstem disease
Detailed oculomotor assessment, with video-oculography where available
Family pedigree analysis and cascade genetic testing with counselling
Nerve conduction studies if a peripheral neuropathy is suspected clinically
Screen for treatable acquired ataxias (vitamin E, thyroid function, coeliac and paraneoplastic antibodies) before settling on a genetic label
redFlags: Rapid deterioration, prominent autonomic failure or early falls suggest multiple system atrophy rather than SCA11.
Marked cognitive decline, seizures or prominent extrapyramidal features are atypical and warrant reconsideration.
New bulbar symptoms such as swallowing difficulty or aspiration require prompt safety assessment.
Acute or subacute onset points to an acquired cause and demands urgent evaluation.
reference.prognosis: SCA11 is generally benign among the dominant ataxias, with slow progression, prolonged independent walking and a normal or near-normal life expectancy, though gait aids may eventually be needed.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal common-expansion panel excludes a dominant ataxia; SCA11 is a rare conventional-mutation cause that requires gene sequencing.
Mislabelling the mild, slowly progressive course as functional or as simple ageing, delaying diagnosis.
Overlooking a subtle dominant family history because of the mild phenotype and variable age at onset.
Attributing pyramidal signs to a separate condition rather than recognising them as part of SCA11.
management: Provide symptomatic care for this mild, largely pure cerebellar ataxia, as no disease-modifying therapy for the TTBK2 mutation is available
Maintain balance and gait with physiotherapy and, when eventually needed, walking aids, given the prolonged preservation of mobility
Offer speech and language therapy for mild dysarthria
Reassure regarding the generally benign course and near-normal life expectancy, with periodic clinical monitoring
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance and cascade testing of relatives
